# Evaluation and Discussion {#sec-chapter5}

The framework developed in @sec-chapter4 ranks six production services from five operational indicators held in the organisation's ITSM instance and CMDB. Before the order is interpreted, it has to earn trust. This chapter therefore tests it from several directions: whether it is stable under varying weights and observation years, whether alternative methods reproduce it, whether it adds information over a single-criterion view, and whether it survives the removal of individual services. A final section reads the rankings against the research questions.

## Evaluation Criteria {#sec-evaluationcriteria}

The framework is evaluated against the criteria set out in @sec-evaluationapproach, forming an analytical evaluation in the sense of @hevnerDesignScienceInformation2004 Guideline 3. Five properties are at issue. Ranking stability asks whether the order survives reasonable weight variation and holds across observation periods, assessed throughout with Kendall's tau ($\tau$). Convergent validity asks whether alternative methods reproduce the ordering, and discriminant value whether the ranking adds anything over a single-criterion incident-frequency baseline. Structural rigour requires the remaining order to hold when any service is removed. Practical validity, finally, asks whether the rankings can be read sensibly against the service profiles they describe.

## Stability Results {#sec-stability}

Kendall's tau measures the similarity between two rankings and is well established in MCDA evaluation [@shekhovtsovHowStronglyRank2021]. It scales concordant minus discordant pairs to $[-1, 1]$, where $\tau = 1$ is perfect agreement. With only six services the p-value is obtained exactly across all $6! = 720$ orderings. The small sample limits the test's power, but the limitation reflects portfolio size rather than weak agreement, since p-values fall as the sample grows when a real effect is present [@chenRolesChallengesMerits2023]. The p-values in @tbl-kendall are therefore read as effect sizes rather than accept-or-reject decisions. All figures refer to the standard formulation; the absolute-mode variant is examined in @sec-absolutemode.

| Comparison | $\tau$ | $p$ |
|------------------|-----------------:|-----------------:|
| Weight sensitivity 2025 (equal vs adjusted) | 0.867 | 0.017 |
| Weight sensitivity 2024 (equal vs adjusted) | 0.733 | 0.056 |
| Temporal stability equal weights (2025 vs 2024) | 0.867| 0.017 |
| Temporal stability adjusted weights (2025 vs 2024) | 1.000 | 0.003 |

: Kendall's tau concordance values across all ranking comparisons, standard TOPSIS formulation. {#tbl-kendall tbl-colwidths="[55,15,15]"}

Weight sensitivity in 2025 is strong ($\tau = 0.867$). The only movement is a swap between SVC-06 and SVC-02 at ranks 2 and 3, as SVC-02's high unsupported component months and weaker patch recency pull it above SVC-06 once those criteria receive more weight. Temporal stability is perfect under adjusted weights ($\tau = 1.000$) and strong under equal weights ($\tau = 0.867$), where only SVC-01 and SVC-05 trade ranks 4 and 5. Cross-year stability is reported as descriptive context rather than as a quality criterion in its own right: services genuinely evolve between periods, and a faithful ranking should follow such change, as this single swap follows a real shift in the two profiles. The weakest result is the 2024 weight sensitivity ($\tau = 0.733$), where two pairs swap because the middle-ranking services carry more tightly grouped scores that year; differential weighting matters more where profiles are similar. In every run, however, the top and bottom positions are identical, which addresses RQ3 directly.

## Convergent Validity Across Methods {#sec-convergent}

To test whether the ordering depends on the choice of method, the six services were re-ranked with SAW and VIKOR and compared against standard TOPSIS. SAW used Weitendorf (min-max) normalisation to avoid the division by zero that classic cost normalisation would produce on the dataset's zero values [@thienOvercomingLimitationsRAPS2024]. VIKOR followed the standard S, R and Q procedure with $v = 0.5$. Full figures are in @sec-appendixc.

Agreement is moderate rather than exact ($\tau$ from 0.600 to 0.867), and the pattern behind the numbers is consistent. All three methods place the same three services in the high-priority half and the same three in the low-priority half, and SVC-03 comes last under every method, configuration and year. They differ only on the internal order of the high-priority cluster: TOPSIS ranks SVC-04 first on its incident volume and CFR, whereas SAW and VIKOR promote SVC-06, whose worst-in-portfolio patch recency and unsupported-component exposure give it the largest single-criterion regret. The broad prioritisation is therefore largely method-independent even where the single top service is not, a distinction revisited in @sec-evaluationlimitations.

## Discriminant Value Against a Single-Criterion Baseline {#sec-discriminant}

A multi-criteria framework only earns its complexity if it says something an obvious single signal would not. Tested against a ranking by incident frequency alone, the orderings diverge ($\tau = 0.600$ in 2025, $0.200$ in 2024; full comparison in @sec-appendixc). The divergence concentrates in two services. SVC-02 rises against the incident-only view because its infrastructure-lifecycle debt, carried in unsupported-component exposure and low patch recency, is invisible to an incident count. SVC-05 falls for the mirror-image reason: high incident volume offset by full patch recency and no unsupported components. This is the value the multi-criteria design adds, consistent with @albarakManagingTechnicalDebt2022. The wider 2024 divergence is the same mechanism operating more strongly.

## Rank Reversal {#sec-rankreversal}

Structural rigour was examined by removing each service in turn and re-ranking the remainder. Under the standard formulation the order holds in three of the six removals; in the other three a single adjacent pair changes places (@tbl-rankreversal). No service crosses between the halves and the lowest-priority service never moves, so the effect is confined to fine ordering within already adjacent clusters. This is the familiar limitation of distance-based aggregation identified by @garcia-cascalesRankReversalTOPSIS2012.

| Service removed | Outcome |
|---|---|
| SVC-01 | Order preserved |
| SVC-02 | SVC-04 and SVC-06 exchange ranks 1 and 2 |
| SVC-03 | Order preserved |
| SVC-04 | SVC-01 and SVC-05 exchange ranks |
| SVC-05 | Order preserved |
| SVC-06 | SVC-01 and SVC-05 exchange ranks |

: Effect of removing each service on the order of the remaining five, standard TOPSIS, 2025 equal weights. {#tbl-rankreversal tbl-colwidths="[35,65]"}

To remove the effect, the absolute-mode correction of @garcia-cascalesRankReversalTOPSIS2012 was implemented. Vector normalisation is replaced by normalisation against fixed criterion bounds, and the ideal solutions are anchored direction-aware to fictitious alternatives at the extremes of each criterion scale, addressing the cost-attribute limitation that @yangIngeniousSolutionRank2020 identify in the original formulation. Under this variant the order is preserved across all six removals (@sec-appendixc), an outcome guaranteed rather than incidental: @yangIngeniousSolutionRank2020 prove that variants whose bounds and ideals are fixed independently of the alternative set are ranking stable by construction. The gain carries a cost, since the fixed bounds must be justified from organisational thresholds rather than sample statistics (values in @sec-appendixa). Anchoring the ranking to a fixed frame, however, changes more than its stability properties.

## Behaviour of the Absolute-Mode Variant {#sec-absolutemode}

The two observation years expose what else changes. In 2025 the absolute-mode variant agrees perfectly with SAW and VIKOR ($\tau = 1.000$ under both weight configurations). In 2024 agreement collapses to $\tau = 0.200$ and $0.333$ respectively, well below the standard formulation's 0.733 and 0.867. The divergence traces almost entirely to SVC-06. SAW and VIKOR rank it first in both years, its VIKOR regret at the maximum throughout, driven by worst-in-portfolio patch recency in both years, joined by unsupported components in 2024 and by change failure rate in 2025. The absolute-mode variant places it fifth in 2024 and first in 2025, its closeness coefficient moving from 0.853 to 0.609.

The mechanism is the interaction between compensation and the reference frame. SAW and VIKOR normalise against the observed portfolio, so a worst-in-sample value is penalised however moderate it is in absolute terms, and VIKOR's regret term deliberately prevents a concentrated weakness being averaged away. Absolute-mode TOPSIS instead measures Euclidean distance to fixed anchors: a deficiency that is worst in the portfolio but moderate on the absolute scale contributes little, and squared aggregation across five criteria lets strong values dilute a single weak one. SVC-06's 2024 debt was concentrated in exactly this way.

Read together, the behaviours are informative rather than contradictory. The sample-relative methods flagged SVC-06's relative weakness in both years; the absolute-mode variant registered it only in 2025, once the deterioration had broadened in absolute magnitude, a movement also visible in VIKOR's utility component rising from 0.491 to 0.559 while its regret stayed capped. The variant's low year-on-year concordance ($\tau = 0.467$ equal, $0.333$ adjusted) follows from the same movement and, per @sec-stability, is not read as a deficiency: the profile genuinely changed on the absolute scale, which only this variant can express, and only its scores remain comparable across periods. The practical consequence is a division of labour. Absolute mode contributes rank-reversal immunity and cross-period comparability, but its compensatory aggregation can mask a deficiency concentrated in one or two criteria, often the signal that matters most in debt prioritisation. It is therefore treated as a complementary perspective, while the standard formulation, triangulated against SAW and VIKOR, remains the primary signal.

## Weight-Space Robustness {#sec-montecarlo}

Because two discrete configurations cannot capture the plurality of defensible judgements a weighting encodes [@grecoMethodologicalFrameworkComposite2019], a Monte Carlo procedure sampled 20,000 weight vectors uniformly from the Dirichlet simplex over the five criteria and recomputed the ranking for each. The absolute-mode scorer is used because each sampled weighting is a distinct decision context, and its set-invariant reference frame (@sec-absolutemode) keeps rank-reversal effects out of the weight-space result. This approximates, in tractable form, the stochastic acceptability analysis those authors advocate. The run is reproducible from a fixed seed; repeating it with a different seed and sample size changed no reported figure by more than 0.01.

@tbl-montecarlo reports the rank-acceptability distribution for 2025, reinforcing the two-vector result across the full weight space. SVC-03 occupies the lowest priority in 99.1% of weightings, and the cluster of SVC-04, SVC-06 and SVC-02 holds the top three positions in the large majority of samples. Sensitivity is localised to the middle of the portfolio, where SVC-01 and SVC-05 exchange positions. The extreme priorities are thus robust to any reasonable weighting, which further addresses RQ3.

| Service | R1 | R2 | R3 | R4 | R5 | R6 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| SVC-01 | 0.0287 | 0.0737 | 0.1224 | 0.3714 | 0.4038 | 0.0000 |
| SVC-02 | 0.2608 | 0.1630 | 0.2790 | 0.1318 | 0.1568 | 0.0088 |
| SVC-03 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0088 | 0.9912 |
| SVC-04 | 0.3412 | 0.3152 | 0.3047 | 0.0390 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |
| SVC-05 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.2008 | 0.4028 | 0.3964 | 0.0000 |
| SVC-06 | 0.3693 | 0.4482 | 0.0931 | 0.0551 | 0.0343 | 0.0000 |

: Rank-acceptability distribution across 20,000 Dirichlet-sampled weight vectors, absolute-mode TOPSIS, 2025, seed 20000. Each cell is the probability of that rank; rows sum to one. {#tbl-montecarlo tbl-colwidths="[22,13,13,13,13,13,13]"}

Repeating the analysis on 2024 data yields a visibly flatter distribution (@tbl-appc-montecarlo2024): SVC-03 occupies the lowest rank in 70.4% of weightings rather than 99.1%, and only SVC-04 retains a dominant top position. This mirrors the weaker 2024 weight-sensitivity result in @sec-stability and has the same cause, the more tightly grouped 2024 profiles, confirming that weight sensitivity here is a property of the data rather than of the method.

## Practical Validity {#sec-practicalvalidity}

Three services illustrate what the rankings capture. SVC-04 holds rank 1 under the standard formulation: its 2025 profile pairs the highest incident frequency (574 per year) with an MTTR of 41.91 hours and a CFR of 3.38, the indicators mapped in @tbl-indicators-lit to architectural, infrastructure/platform and process debt [@detoledoReducingIncidentsMicroservices2021; @nordExamplesTechnicalDebts2021], while exhibiting no unsupported components and full patch recency. Its debt is therefore concentrated in the dimensions that manifest in delivery and recovery performance rather than in infrastructure lifecycle or vulnerability debt [@hakiDigitalNudgingTechnical2023]. SVC-03 has the lowest priority in every run, with the fewest incidents, low MTTR and CFR, full patch recency and no unsupported components, and offers a concrete reference for a well-maintained service. The most revealing case is SVC-02: third under equal weights and second under adjusted weights, driven by an unsupported component months value of 1,221, by far the largest in the portfolio, together with a patch recency of 59.93, the second lowest recorded. This is the signal the framework is built to surface, a service that looks stable in isolation but carries structural debt that only multi-criteria analysis brings into view [@hakiDigitalNudgingTechnical2023]. A fourth case, SVC-06, is discussed in @sec-absolutemode, where the methods disagree about it in an instructive way.

These results address RQ2. A cross-sectional design cannot establish whether the observed metrics are downstream effects of technical debt severity or arise from other operational factors, so proxy validity is assessed on the basis of convergence with theory rather than demonstrated causal mechanism. The rankings match the debt profiles the literature predicts for each position [@hakiDigitalNudgingTechnical2023; @ramasubbuControllingTechnicalDebt2021; @nordExamplesTechnicalDebts2021], yielding an ordinal signal readable against @tbl-indicators-lit.

## Limitations of the Evaluation {#sec-evaluationlimitations}

Every strand of the evaluation draws on the same dataset and indicator set used to build the framework, so the triangulation and baseline comparisons establish convergent and discriminant validity but not criterion validity against an independent measure of technical debt, for which none exists for the non-code debt in scope. External validation is the main avenue for future work. The six-service portfolio also limits the power of the Kendall's tau tests, since $\tau = 0.733$ cannot reach conventional significance across only 720 permutations even where agreement is substantively meaningful. The method disagreement documented in @sec-convergent and @sec-absolutemode adds a further boundary: the framework supports cluster-level confidence, but whether SVC-04 or SVC-06 deserves the single first remediation slot depends on whether concentrated infrastructure-lifecycle exposure is judged more urgent than diffuse architectural and process debt, a managerial judgement the framework informs rather than settles. Finally, the cross-sectional design captures a single snapshot, so a service mid-remediation may look worse than warranted and one whose debt is still growing may not yet show its full consequences; longitudinal evaluation is flagged in @sec-chapter6, and the data quality limitations in @sec-datalimitations apply here, with middle-position rankings in particular warranting careful reading.
